notes.topic: Introduction to Linear Algebra and Systems of Equations
notes.summary: This lecture introduces the fundamentals of linear algebra by exploring systems of linear equations through both row and column perspectives. It extends these geometric interpretations from two-dimensional spaces to three-dimensional examples involving intersecting planes and linear combinations of vectors. Finally, it examines singular cases with dependent columns and demonstrates how matrix-vector multiplication represents combinations of column vectors.

cornell_notes.cue: What is the fundamental problem of linear algebra covered in this course?
cornell_notes.note: The fundamental problem is to solve a system of linear equations. In the normal, nice case, this involves an equal number of equations and unknowns, denoted as n equations and n unknowns.

cornell_notes.cue: How are linear equations represented in matrix form?
cornell_notes.note: A system of linear equations is written compactly as Ax equals b. Here, A is the coefficient matrix containing the numerical coefficients in a rectangular array, x is the vector of unknowns, and b is the vector representing the right-hand side values.

cornell_notes.cue: What does the row picture represent in a 2x2 system?
cornell_notes.note: The row picture looks at one equation at a time, where each equation in a two-variable system forms a straight line in the x-y plane. The solution to the system is the single all-important point where these lines intersect.

cornell_notes.cue: What is a linear combination of columns?
cornell_notes.note: A linear combination involves taking the columns of the matrix A, multiplying each by a scalar (the components of the vector x), and adding them together. This is considered the most fundamental operation in the entire course.

cornell_notes.cue: How is the column picture visualized geometrically?
cornell_notes.note: Instead of intersecting lines, the column picture is visualized by placing vector arrows head-to-tail. You scale the column vectors by the unknown values and chain them together to reach the final right-hand side vector b.

cornell_notes.cue: How is a three-by-three linear system represented in matrix form?
cornell_notes.note: A 3x3 system consists of three equations with three unknowns (x, y, and z), which can be written in shorthand as Ax = b. The matrix A is formed by the coefficients of the variables across its three rows and columns, and b is the vector representing the right-hand side values.

cornell_notes.cue: What is the geometric interpretation of the row picture in three dimensions?
cornell_notes.note: In the row picture, each individual linear equation represents a plane in three-dimensional space. Two equations intersect to form a line, and a third non-parallel plane typically intersects that line at a single point, which represents the solution to the system.

cornell_notes.cue: Why might the row picture become difficult to use?
cornell_notes.note: While sketching two lines intersecting is straightforward, visualizing three intersecting planes in three dimensions can become unclear and hard to draw. In higher dimensions like four-space, visualizing planes becomes even more difficult, prompting the need for alternative approaches.

cornell_notes.cue: What does the column picture represent in a linear system?
cornell_notes.note: The column picture reframes the matrix equation Ax = b as finding a linear combination of the columns of matrix A using the variables as weights to produce the right-hand side vector b. Each column acts as a three-dimensional vector that must be combined to hit the target b.

cornell_notes.cue: How can a solution be identified directly from the column picture?
cornell_notes.note: If the right-hand side vector b happens to match one of the columns of matrix A, the solution is immediately apparent by inspection. For instance, setting the corresponding variable multiplier to one and all other multipliers to zero yields the target vector.

cornell_notes.cue: What core question is asked when considering the big picture for all right-hand sides?
cornell_notes.note: The fundamental algebra question asks whether the system AX = b can be solved for every possible right-hand side vector b. In linear combination terms, this asks whether all possible linear combinations of the columns can completely fill three-dimensional space.

cornell_notes.cue: What happens if the columns of matrix A lie in the same plane?
cornell_notes.note: If all three column vectors happen to lie in the same plane, their linear combinations will also be restricted to that same plane rather than filling three-dimensional space. In such a scenario, certain right-hand side vectors cannot be reached, and the answer to whether you can solve for every b becomes no.

cornell_notes.cue: When does a matrix system fail to produce every possible right-hand side B?
cornell_notes.note: A system fails when the columns of the matrix all lie in the same plane, meaning their linear combinations also remain confined to that plane. For example, if a third column is simply the sum of the first and second columns, it contributes nothing new. Consequently, any right-hand side vector lying outside that plane will be unreachable, resulting in a singular, non-invertible matrix.

cornell_notes.cue: How can we conceptualize matrices and linear combinations in nine dimensions?
cornell_notes.note: While nine-dimensional vectors cannot be easily visualized, we can pretend to work with them by imagining nine equations and nine unknowns. If we pick a random matrix using software like MATLAB, it is almost guaranteed to be non-singular and invertible, successfully spanning the entire nine-dimensional space. However, if columns are dependent—such as the ninth column matching the eighth—the combinations will instead fill out a lower-dimensional plane inside the nine-dimensional space.

cornell_notes.cue: What are the two ways to interpret matrix-vector multiplication $Ax$?
cornell_notes.note: Matrix multiplication can be computed either by columns or by rows. The author's favorite perspective views the product as a linear combination of the matrix's columns, where the components of vector x dictate how much of each column to add together. Alternatively, it can be computed a row at a time using the dot product of each row vector with the input vector x.

cornell_notes.cue: How is a matrix-vector multiplication calculated using columns?
cornell_notes.note: To multiply a matrix by a vector using the column method, you take scalar multiples of each matrix column corresponding to the entries in the vector and sum them up. For instance, multiplying a 2x2 matrix with columns by a vector with entries 1 and 2 means taking one of the first column and two of the second column, then adding them together to yield the resulting vector.

cornell_notes.cue: What is the row-based approach to matrix multiplication called?
cornell_notes.note: The row-based approach involves multiplying each row of the matrix by the vector x, an operation that will later be formally defined as a dot product. Each resulting scalar forms a component of the final output vector. Both methods yield the exact same numerical result, but the column view emphasizes linear combinations.

mcqs.question: What does the row picture of a two-variable linear equation represent in the x-y plane?
options: A vector starting at the origin

mcqs.question: In the matrix equation Ax = b, what does the matrix A represent?
What is described as the most fundamental operation in the entire course?
options: Finding the determinant of a matrix
A linear combination of the columns
Plotting lines in the x-y plane
mcqs.answer: A linear combination of the columns

mcqs.question: For the specific 2x2 example discussed, what is the solution point (x, y) that lies on both lines?
In the row picture for a 3x3 system of linear equations, what does each individual equation geometrically represent?
How is the matrix equation Ax = b interpreted in the column picture?
options: As finding the intersection of three planes
As taking linear combinations of the columns of A to produce b
As multiplying the right-hand side by the inverse of each row
As finding the determinant of the three-by-three matrix
mcqs.answer: As taking linear combinations of the columns of A to produce b

mcqs.question: What causes the column picture to fail in producing every possible right-hand side vector b?
options: When the columns are all equal to zero
When the three columns all lie in the same plane
When the right-hand side vector has four components
When the matrix is too small to compute
mcqs.answer: When the three columns all lie in the same plane

mcqs.question: What systematic method is introduced as the upcoming topic for solving equations in all cases?
What causes a matrix to be singular and non-invertible in terms of its columns?
options: When all columns have equal scalar values.
When the columns lie in the same plane and do not provide new independent directions.
When the matrix has more rows than columns.
When the right-hand side vector B is a zero vector.
mcqs.answer: When the columns lie in the same plane and do not provide new independent directions.

mcqs.question: What typically happens if you generate a random 9x9 matrix in MATLAB?
options: It will guarantee a non-singular and invertible matrix.
It will fail to produce any right-hand side vectors.
Its columns will automatically lie in the same plane.
mcqs.answer: It will guarantee a non-singular and invertible matrix.

mcqs.question: How does the lecturer primarily prefer to think about the matrix-vector product Ax?
options: As a set of independent scalar additions
As a linear combination of the columns of A
As an inversion of the vector x
As a cross product of rows and columns
mcqs.answer: As a linear combination of the columns of A

mcqs.question: When computing matrix multiplication by rows, what operation is being performed on each row with the vector x?

# Introduction to Linear Algebra and Systems of Equations

## Summary

This lecture introduces the fundamentals of linear algebra by exploring systems of linear equations through both row and column perspectives. It extends these geometric interpretations from two-dimensional spaces to three-dimensional examples involving intersecting planes and linear combinations of vectors. Finally, it examines singular cases with dependent columns and demonstrates how matrix-vector multiplication represents combinations of column vectors.

## Cornell Notes

| Cue | Notes |
|---|---|
| What is the fundamental problem of linear algebra covered in this course? *(0:57)* | The fundamental problem is to solve a system of linear equations. In the normal, nice case, this involves an equal number of equations and unknowns, denoted as n equations and n unknowns. |
| How are linear equations represented in matrix form? *(2:53)* | A system of linear equations is written compactly as Ax equals b. Here, A is the coefficient matrix containing the numerical coefficients in a rectangular array, x is the vector of unknowns, and b is the vector representing the right-hand side values. |
| What does the row picture represent in a 2x2 system? *(4:24)* | The row picture looks at one equation at a time, where each equation in a two-variable system forms a straight line in the x-y plane. The solution to the system is the single all-important point where these lines intersect. |
| What is a linear combination of columns? *(9:51)* | A linear combination involves taking the columns of the matrix A, multiplying each by a scalar (the components of the vector x), and adding them together. This is considered the most fundamental operation in the entire course. |
| How is the column picture visualized geometrically? *(12:21)* | Instead of intersecting lines, the column picture is visualized by placing vector arrows head-to-tail. You scale the column vectors by the unknown values and chain them together to reach the final right-hand side vector b. |
| How is a three-by-three linear system represented in matrix form? *(16:41)* | A 3x3 system consists of three equations with three unknowns (x, y, and z), which can be written in shorthand as Ax = b. The matrix A is formed by the coefficients of the variables across its three rows and columns, and b is the vector representing the right-hand side values. |
| What is the geometric interpretation of the row picture in three dimensions? *(17:32)* | In the row picture, each individual linear equation represents a plane in three-dimensional space. Two equations intersect to form a line, and a third non-parallel plane typically intersects that line at a single point, which represents the solution to the system. |
| Why might the row picture become difficult to use? *(21:11)* | While sketching two lines intersecting is straightforward, visualizing three intersecting planes in three dimensions can become unclear and hard to draw. In higher dimensions like four-space, visualizing planes becomes even more difficult, prompting the need for alternative approaches. |
| What does the column picture represent in a linear system? *(22:04)* | The column picture reframes the matrix equation Ax = b as finding a linear combination of the columns of matrix A using the variables as weights to produce the right-hand side vector b. Each column acts as a three-dimensional vector that must be combined to hit the target b. |
| How can a solution be identified directly from the column picture? *(24:33)* | If the right-hand side vector b happens to match one of the columns of matrix A, the solution is immediately apparent by inspection. For instance, setting the corresponding variable multiplier to one and all other multipliers to zero yields the target vector. |
| What core question is asked when considering the big picture for all right-hand sides? *(27:48)* | The fundamental algebra question asks whether the system AX = b can be solved for every possible right-hand side vector b. In linear combination terms, this asks whether all possible linear combinations of the columns can completely fill three-dimensional space. |
| What happens if the columns of matrix A lie in the same plane? *(30:38)* | If all three column vectors happen to lie in the same plane, their linear combinations will also be restricted to that same plane rather than filling three-dimensional space. In such a scenario, certain right-hand side vectors cannot be reached, and the answer to whether you can solve for every b becomes no. |
| When does a matrix system fail to produce every possible right-hand side B? *(31:00)* | A system fails when the columns of the matrix all lie in the same plane, meaning their linear combinations also remain confined to that plane. For example, if a third column is simply the sum of the first and second columns, it contributes nothing new. Consequently, any right-hand side vector lying outside that plane will be unreachable, resulting in a singular, non-invertible matrix. |
| How can we conceptualize matrices and linear combinations in nine dimensions? *(32:26)* | While nine-dimensional vectors cannot be easily visualized, we can pretend to work with them by imagining nine equations and nine unknowns. If we pick a random matrix using software like MATLAB, it is almost guaranteed to be non-singular and invertible, successfully spanning the entire nine-dimensional space. However, if columns are dependent—such as the ninth column matching the eighth—the combinations will instead fill out a lower-dimensional plane inside the nine-dimensional space. |
| What are the two ways to interpret matrix-vector multiplication $Ax$? *(36:45)* | Matrix multiplication can be computed either by columns or by rows. The author's favorite perspective views the product as a linear combination of the matrix's columns, where the components of vector x dictate how much of each column to add together. Alternatively, it can be computed a row at a time using the dot product of each row vector with the input vector x. |
| How is a matrix-vector multiplication calculated using columns? *(36:52)* | To multiply a matrix by a vector using the column method, you take scalar multiples of each matrix column corresponding to the entries in the vector and sum them up. For instance, multiplying a 2x2 matrix with columns by a vector with entries 1 and 2 means taking one of the first column and two of the second column, then adding them together to yield the resulting vector. |
| What is the row-based approach to matrix multiplication called? *(37:37)* | The row-based approach involves multiplying each row of the matrix by the vector x, an operation that will later be formally defined as a dot product. Each resulting scalar forms a component of the final output vector. Both methods yield the exact same numerical result, but the column view emphasizes linear combinations. |

## Practice Questions

1. What does the row picture of a two-variable linear equation represent in the x-y plane?
   - A. A straight line of solutions
   - B. A single isolated point
   - C. A vector starting at the origin
   - D. A three-dimensional plane

2. In the matrix equation Ax = b, what does the matrix A represent?
   - A. The vector of unknowns
   - B. The coefficient matrix
   - C. The right-hand side vector
   - D. The inverse of the system

3. What is described as the most fundamental operation in the entire course?
   - A. Finding the determinant of a matrix
   - B. Inverting a matrix
   - C. A linear combination of the columns
   - D. Plotting lines in the x-y plane

4. For the specific 2x2 example discussed, what is the solution point (x, y) that lies on both lines?
   - A. x = 0, y = 3
   - B. x = -1, y = 1
   - C. x = 1, y = 2
   - D. x = -3, y = 0

5. In the row picture for a 3x3 system of linear equations, what does each individual equation geometrically represent?
   - A. A line in three-dimensional space
   - B. A plane in three-dimensional space
   - C. A single point in space
   - D. A three-dimensional vector

6. How is the matrix equation Ax = b interpreted in the column picture?
   - A. As finding the intersection of three planes
   - B. As taking linear combinations of the columns of A to produce b
   - C. As multiplying the right-hand side by the inverse of each row
   - D. As finding the determinant of the three-by-three matrix

7. What causes the column picture to fail in producing every possible right-hand side vector b?
   - A. When the columns are all equal to zero
   - B. When the three columns all lie in the same plane
   - C. When the right-hand side vector has four components
   - D. When the matrix is too small to compute

8. What systematic method is introduced as the upcoming topic for solving equations in all cases?
   - A. Elimination
   - B. Differentiation
   - C. Approximation
   - D. Integration

9. What causes a matrix to be singular and non-invertible in terms of its columns?
   - A. When all columns have equal scalar values.
   - B. When the columns lie in the same plane and do not provide new independent directions.
   - C. When the matrix has more rows than columns.
   - D. When the right-hand side vector B is a zero vector.

10. What typically happens if you generate a random 9x9 matrix in MATLAB?
   - A. It will always be singular.
   - B. It will guarantee a non-singular and invertible matrix.
   - C. It will fail to produce any right-hand side vectors.
   - D. Its columns will automatically lie in the same plane.

11. How does the lecturer primarily prefer to think about the matrix-vector product Ax?
   - A. As a set of independent scalar additions
   - B. As a linear combination of the columns of A
   - C. As an inversion of the vector x
   - D. As a cross product of rows and columns

12. When computing matrix multiplication by rows, what operation is being performed on each row with the vector x?
   - A. A dot product
   - B. A cross product
   - C. A matrix inversion
   - D. A vector normalization

<details><summary>Answer key</summary>

1. A — A straight line of solutions
2. B — The coefficient matrix
3. C — A linear combination of the columns
4. C — x = 1, y = 2
5. B — A plane in three-dimensional space
6. B — As taking linear combinations of the columns of A to produce b
7. B — When the three columns all lie in the same plane
8. A — Elimination
9. B — When the columns lie in the same plane and do not provide new independent directions.
10. B — It will guarantee a non-singular and invertible matrix.
11. B — As a linear combination of the columns of A
12. A — A dot product

</details>
